the_employees_provident_fund_epf_or_kwsp:
The Employees Provident Fund (EPF), or KWSP, is a mandatory
            retirement savings scheme in Malaysia designed to ensure long-term
            financial security for employees. Both workers and employers
            contribute a portion of the monthly salary into the individual's
            account.
_retirement_planning_and_postcareer_inco: • Retirement planning and post-career income
_housing_withdrawals_for_home_purchases_: • Housing withdrawals for home purchases or loan repayments
_education_expenses_for_yourself_or_your: • Education expenses for yourself or your children
_medical_support_and_emergency_financial: • Medical support and emergency financial needs
contributions_are_automatically_deducted:
Contributions are automatically deducted from your monthly gross
            salary. The rates are statutory but vary based on age, monthly
            income level, and citizenship status.
a_standard_percentage_usually_11_for_tho:
A standard percentage (usually 11% for those below 60) is
                deducted directly from your monthly payslip.
employers_provide_an_additional_contribu:
Employers provide an additional contribution (12% to 13%) on top
                of your base salary, deposited into your account.
calculation_is_simple_multiply_your_gros:
Calculation is simple: multiply your gross monthly salary by the
            applicable employee and employer rates. For most Malaysians earning
            below RM5,000, the employer rate is 13%.
reference_table_for_standard_monthly_con:
Reference table for standard monthly contribution amounts based on
            gross income for Malaysian citizens below age 60.
epf_contributions_are_legally_mandatory_:
EPF contributions are legally mandatory for all eligible employees
            in Malaysia. Failure to comply can result in significant legal
            consequences for employers.
yes_employers_who_fail_to_contribute_by_:
Yes. Employers who fail to contribute by the 15th of each month
                face heavy fines, penalties, and potential legal action.
_all_fulltime_and_parttime_employees_are: • All full-time and part-time employees are covered.
_foreign_workers_and_noncitizens_can_als: • Foreign workers and non-citizens can also contribute voluntarily.
epf_contributions_are_calculated_based_o: EPF contributions are calculated based on your gross monthly salary, age group and nationality. Both employee and employer contribute every month.
yes_members_can_make_partial_or_full_wit: Yes. Members can make partial or full withdrawals prior to retirement under specified EPF schemes:
account_3_akaun_fleksibel_instant_flexib: Account 3 (Akaun Fleksibel): Instant, flexible withdrawals anytime for any purpose with no conditions.
account_2_akaun_sejahtera_approved_prere: Account 2 (Akaun Sejahtera): Approved pre-retirement withdrawals for housing, education, medical expenses, Hajj, or age 50.
full_withdrawal_permitted_upon_reaching_: Full Withdrawal: Permitted upon reaching age 55, incapacitation, or permanent departure from Malaysia.
your_accumulated_epf_savings_remain_comp: Your accumulated EPF savings remain completely secure and intact:
account_continuity_your_epf_member_numbe: Account Continuity: Your EPF member number remains unchanged throughout your career across all private-sector employers.
seamless_onboarding_simply_provide_your_: Seamless Onboarding: Simply provide your existing EPF member number to your new employer upon joining.
dividend_accumulation_existing_account_b: Dividend Accumulation: Existing account balances continue earning annual compounded EPF dividends uninterrupted.
epf_contributions_are_governed_by_statut: EPF contributions are governed by statutory guidelines depending on residency status:
malaysian_citizens_prs_mandatory_at_stan: Malaysian Citizens & PRs: Mandatory at standard statutory rates (11% employee / 12-13% employer).

how_accurate_are_these_calculations_all_:
How accurate are these calculations?

All calculations strictly adhere to official schedules published by statutory government bodies:

  • Statutory Accuracy: Follows exact contribution tables and formulas from KWSP (EPF), PERKESO (SOCSO & EIS), and LHDN (PCB income tax).
  • Latest Rates: Updated for the current tax year including wage ceilings and tax relief brackets.
Note: Results are estimates. Actual payslip amounts may vary slightly due to company-specific allowance taxability, individual relief claims, or special exemptions.
Is my salary data saved anywhere?

No. Your privacy is fully guaranteed during every session:

  • Client-Side Processing: Every calculation runs 100% locally inside your browser.
  • Zero Data Stored: We maintain 0 data stored — no tracking, database logging, or external analytics on your financial inputs.
  • Complete Confidentiality: Your salary details never leave your device.
What should I enter as gross salary?

Gross salary represents total pre-deduction earnings:

  • Base Monthly Pay: Enter your basic salary before any statutory deductions.
  • Fixed Allowances: Include recurring fixed monthly allowances (e.g., transport, housing, position allowances).
  • Variable Earnings: Exclude one-off bonuses or irregular overtime; use the dedicated Bonus / Allowance input fields for variable pay.
Why is my PCB showing RM0?

Monthly Tax Deduction (PCB) only applies once chargeable income exceeds mandatory income thresholds:

  • Single Individuals: Income after EPF must exceed RM 2,851 / month.
  • Married Individuals: Threshold rises to RM 3,851 / month (with non-working spouse).
  • Tax Relief Reductions: Personal, medical, and child tax reliefs further lower your monthly PCB deduction.
Important: Even if your monthly PCB deduction is RM 0, you may still need to file an annual income tax return with LHDN via MyTax if your total annual income exceeds RM 34,000.
Why does SOCSO stop at RM6,000?

Statutory contributions for social security have a fixed maximum threshold:

  • Statutory Wage Ceiling: Both PERKESO (SOCSO) and EIS contributions are capped at the RM 6,000 wage limit.
  • Capped Rate: Earnings above RM 6,000 / month pay the exact same fixed maximum contribution as an RM 6,000 salary.
  • Updated Regulation: The ceiling was enforced by PERKESO in October 2024 (up from RM 5,000).
Does this calculator work for foreigners?

Yes. Select Foreigner / Non-Malaysian under Nationality settings:

  • Foreigner EPF Rate: Foreign employees are subject to mandatory EPF contributions at 2% employee + 2% employer.
  • Non-Resident PCB Tax: Charged at a flat 30% rate unless tax residency (182+ days in Malaysia) is established with LHDN.
  • Exemptions: EIS contributions do not apply to foreign employees.
How often are the rates updated?

We continuously maintain alignment with official government policies:

  • Annual Tax Sync: Updated every January to incorporate new Budget tax reliefs and LHDN formulas.
  • Immediate Gazette Sync: Mid-year statutory updates (such as the RM 6,000 SOCSO ceiling or EPF rate updates) are applied immediately upon enforcement by KWSP and PERKESO.
What is the difference between employee and employer contributions?

Statutory contributions are split between payroll deductions and employer costs:

  • Employee Deductions: Subtracted directly from gross salary, reducing your net take-home pay.
  • Employer Contributions: Paid separately by your company directly to KWSP, PERKESO, and EIS without reducing your gross pay.
  • Total Cost of Employment (TCOE): Represents the complete financial expenditure required by an employer (Gross Salary + Employer Statutory Contributions).

can_i_withdraw_my_epf_savings_before_ret:
Can I withdraw my EPF savings before retirement?

Yes. Members can make partial or full withdrawals prior to retirement under specified EPF schemes:

  • Account 3 (Akaun Fleksibel): Instant, flexible withdrawals anytime for any purpose with no conditions.
  • Account 2 (Akaun Sejahtera): Approved pre-retirement withdrawals for housing, education, medical expenses, Hajj, or age 50.
  • Full Withdrawal: Permitted upon reaching age 55, incapacitation, or permanent departure from Malaysia.
What happens to my EPF if I resign or change jobs?

Your accumulated EPF savings remain completely secure and intact:

  • Account Continuity: Your EPF member number remains unchanged throughout your career across all private-sector employers.
  • Seamless Onboarding: Simply provide your existing EPF member number to your new employer upon joining.
  • Dividend Accumulation: Existing account balances continue earning annual compounded EPF dividends uninterrupted.
Is EPF contribution mandatory for all employees?

EPF contributions are governed by statutory guidelines depending on residency status:

  • Malaysian Citizens & PRs: Mandatory at standard statutory rates (11% employee / 12-13% employer).
  • Non-Citizens & Foreign Workers: Mandatory starting at a minimum rate of 2% employee + 2% employer contributions.
  • Self-Employed & Gig Workers: Voluntary contributions available via i-Saraan with government matching incentives.
Can I contribute more than the standard EPF rate?

Yes! Both employees and employers can voluntarily elect to contribute above standard rates:

  • Voluntary Employee Rate: Submit Form KWSP 17A (AHL) to increase your monthly payroll deduction rate.
  • Voluntary Employer Rate: Employers can choose to contribute higher employer rates as part of competitive remuneration packages.
  • Self-Deposit (i-Akaun): Make voluntary personal contributions anytime up to RM 100,000 annually.
  • Tax Savings: Maximizes eligible individual income tax relief under EPF and life insurance categories.
What is the difference between EPF Account 1, Account 2, and Account 3?

Monthly contributions are split across three dedicated accounts under EPF's restructured 3-Account system:

  • Account 1 (Akaun Persaraan - 75%): Designated for retirement wealth accumulation until reaching age 55.
  • Account 2 (Akaun Sejahtera - 15%): Allocated for pre-retirement life requirements including housing, healthcare, education, and age 50 withdrawals.
  • Account 3 (Akaun Fleksibel - 10%): Accessible anytime for emergency or immediate short-term financial needs with zero conditions.

what_happens_if_my_employer_doesn_t_pay_:
What happens if my employer doesn't pay SOCSO contributions?

Non-compliance with statutory PERKESO contribution regulations incurs strict statutory penalties under the Employees' Social Security Act 1969:

  • Legal Penalties: Non-compliant employers face fines of up to RM10,000 fine, imprisonment of up to 2 years imprisonment, or both.
  • Loss of Coverage: Failure to pay compromises employee eligibility for vital Employment Injury Scheme and Invalidity Scheme protection.
  • Reporting Non-Compliance: Employees can report non-paying employers online via PERKESO's ASSIST Portal or by visiting any physical PERKESO branch nationwide.
Can I withdraw my SOCSO contributions like EPF?

No. Unlike KWSP (EPF), SOCSO functions strictly as a mandatory social insurance scheme rather than an individual savings account:

  • No Lump-Sum Withdrawals: Contributions pooled into national protection funds cannot be withdrawn upon resignation, retirement, or job change.
  • Claim-Based Benefits: Financial payouts and medical benefits are disbursed only upon filing valid claims under the Employment Injury Scheme or Invalidity Scheme.
  • Comprehensive Protection: Provides lifelong medical treatment, temporary/permanent disablement allowances, pensions, and dependants' benefits following workplace accidents or severe illnesses.
Does SOCSO coverage continue after I resign?

No. Standard employment-based coverage ends once active contributions cease, subject to specific claim conditions:

  • Active Employment Term: Standard protection under the Employment Injury Scheme ends on your last day of employment.
  • Historical Claims: You remain eligible to file claims for injuries, occupational diseases, or disabilities incurred during your period of active coverage.
  • New Job Continuation: Your new employer automatically resumes contributions under your existing PERKESO registration.
Are self-employed and gig workers eligible for SOCSO?

Yes! Self-employed workers, e-hailing drivers, delivery riders, and freelancers are covered under dedicated statutory protection:

  • Self-Employment Social Security Scheme (SKSPS): Enables self-employed individuals and gig workers to register and contribute voluntarily.
  • Occupational Protection: Provides medical, temporary disablement, permanent disablement, and dependants' benefits tailored for independent work environments.
  • Online Registration: Convenient enrollment and contribution payments can be processed directly via the PERKESO Matrix Portal or ASSIST Portal.
Does SOCSO cover foreign workers in Malaysia?

Yes. Protection under PERKESO is mandatory for all documented non-citizens and foreign workers:

  • Mandatory Registration: Employers are legally required to register and contribute for all foreign employees under the Employees' Social Security Act 1969.
  • Employment Injury Scheme: Covers foreign workers against workplace accidents, commuting accidents, and occupational diseases.
  • Contribution Rates: Employers contribute 1.25% of the foreign employee's monthly wage, while foreign employees are exempt from employee-side deductions.

What is the difference between PCB and income tax?

PCB (Potongan Cukai Bulanan) is your monthly income tax deduction paid to LHDN by your employer. It is an advance payment of your annual income tax. Any overpayment may be refunded after you file your tax return.

What happens if my employer does not deduct PCB?

Employers must deduct and submit PCB to LHDN. If they fail to do so, penalties may apply. Employees are still responsible for declaring and paying any tax due when filing their annual tax return.

Can I reduce my PCB deduction?

Yes. Declaring eligible tax reliefs or making voluntary EPF contributions may reduce your monthly PCB deduction.

Do I still need to file a tax return if PCB has been deducted?

Yes. Most employees should still submit their annual LHDN tax return to confirm their tax liability, claim reliefs, and receive any eligible refund.

When does PCB start being deducted?

PCB generally starts when your estimated annual chargeable income exceeds the tax threshold set by LHDN. The exact amount depends on your salary and personal tax reliefs.

how_do_you_calculate_pro_rated_annual_le:
How do you calculate pro-rated annual leave in Malaysia?

The formula is (Months Worked ÷ 12) × Annual Leave Entitlement.

Can annual leave expire in Malaysia?

Yes, unless company policy allows carry-forward, unutilized annual leave typically expires.

Can employers reject annual leave?

Yes, employers can approve or reject based on operational needs, provided they adhere to the minimum notice periods.

Is unused annual leave paid after resignation?

Under the Employment Act, an employer must compensate you for unused pro-rated annual leave balance.

Does annual leave include weekends?

No, annual leave only counts towards working days. Rest days do not count.

Is annual leave mandatory in Malaysia?

Yes, under the Employment Act 1955, employees must be given a minimum amount (8 to 16 days depending on tenure).

how_is_overtime_pay_calculated_in_malays:
How is overtime pay calculated in Malaysia?

Overtime pay calculation is governed by the Employment Act 1955 based on your Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) and statutory multipliers:

Overtime Pay Formula: HRP × Overtime Hours × Statutory Multiplier
  • Normal Workday OT: Paid at 1.5x HRP for work exceeding standard daily hours.
  • Rest Day OT (Excess Hours): Paid at 2.0x HRP for work beyond normal rest day schedule.
  • Public Holiday OT (Excess Hours): Paid at 3.0x HRP for work beyond standard public holiday hours.
Is overtime calculated using basic salary or gross salary?

Statutory overtime calculation uses the Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP) rather than total gross salary:

  • Included Earnings: Basic Monthly Salary plus fixed, non-variable monthly allowances (e.g., position or fixed housing allowance).
  • Excluded Earnings: Performance-based bonuses, variable commissions, traveling allowances, and expense reimbursements.
  • Statutory Formula: Calculated using the mandatory fixed 26-day monthly divisor under the Employment Act 1955.
Who is entitled to overtime pay?

Under First Schedule amendments to Malaysia's Employment Act 1955, statutory OT coverage includes:

  • Salary Threshold: Employees earning a basic monthly salary of RM 4,000 or below are statutorily entitled to overtime pay.
  • Manual Labor Exception: Employees engaged in manual labor, supervision of manual workers, or operation of mechanically propelled vehicles are eligible regardless of salary level.
  • Above RM 4,000 Non-Manual: Subject to individual employment contracts or company policy rather than mandatory statutory rates.
What is the overtime rate for public holidays?

Working on an officially gazetted Public Holiday is compensated based on working hours:

  • Within Normal Working Hours: Entitled to 2 days' Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP) regardless of actual hours worked within standard shift.
  • Excess / Overtime Hours: Paid at 3.0x your Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) for every hour worked beyond normal shift hours.
What is the overtime rate for rest days?

Work performed on a scheduled weekly Rest Day follows statutory tiered rates:

  • Up to Half Normal Hours: Paid 0.5 day's ORP (for monthly paid employees).
  • More Than Half Up to Full Shift: Paid 1.0 day's ORP.
  • Excess / Overtime Hours: Paid at 2.0x your Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) for any hours worked beyond standard shift duration.
How do I calculate my hourly rate?

Your Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) is calculated in two steps using statutory Employment Act guidelines:

  • Step 1 — Daily Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP):
    ORP = Monthly Basic Salary ÷ 26
  • Step 2 — Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP):
    HRP = ORP ÷ Normal Daily Working Hours (e.g., 8 hours)
What is the maximum overtime hours allowed per month?

Malaysia enforces strict statutory limits on monthly overtime work under Employment Regulations:

  • Monthly OT Cap: Maximum allowable overtime is 104 hours / month.
  • Exemption Requirements: Employers requiring employees to exceed 104 OT hours must obtain prior written approval from the Director General of Labour (JTK).
  • Weekly Working Hour Limit: Total regular weekly working hours are capped at 45 hours / week under updated Employment Act 1955 standards.

what_is_an_hourly_rate_an_hourly_rate_is:
What is an hourly rate?

An hourly rate is the specific amount of compensation earned for each hour of work performed. It is used to calculate:

  • Part-Time Wages: Hourly compensation for retail, F&B, and contract staff.
  • Freelance Client Invoicing: Billable project rates for contractors and freelancers.
  • Statutory Overtime Pay (OT): Base Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) under the Employment Act 1955.
How do I calculate hourly pay?

The calculation depends on whether you follow statutory labor law or personal schedule methods:

  • Statutory EA 1955 Method: Enforces a fixed 26-day monthly divisor.
    Hourly Rate (HRP) = (Monthly Basic Salary ÷ 26) ÷ Daily Working Hours
  • Calendar Schedule Method: Calculates schedule-based actual monthly working hours.
    Hourly Rate = Monthly Basic Salary ÷ Total Monthly Working Hours
How many working days are there in a month?

Average working days per month vary based on weekly schedule:

  • 5-Day Workweek: Approximately 21.67 working days per month (5 days × 52 weeks ÷ 12 months).
  • 5.5-Day Workweek: Approximately 23.83 working days per month (5.5 days × 52 weeks ÷ 12 months).
  • 6-Day Workweek: Approximately 26.00 working days per month (6 days × 52 weeks ÷ 12 months).
  • Statutory Employment Act (EA 1955): Strictly fixed at 26 days for daily and hourly rates.
Does hourly pay include overtime?

No. Standard hourly rates cover regular working hours only. Overtime hours are compensated using statutory multipliers under the Employment Act 1955:

  • Normal Workday OT: Paid at 1.5x your Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP).
  • Rest Day OT: Paid at 2.0x your HRP for excess hours.
  • Public Holiday OT: Paid at 3.0x your HRP for excess hours.
What is Malaysia's minimum hourly wage?

Under Malaysia's statutory Minimum Wage Order, the minimum monthly base is RM 1,700. Key statutory minimum benchmarks include:

  • Statutory Minimum Hourly Rate: RM 8.17 / hour (based on 8-hour daily shift).
  • Statutory Daily Rate (ORP): RM 65.38 / day (RM 1,700 ÷ 26 days).
  • Monthly Minimum Salary Base: RM 1,700 / month.
